title: An Hour on the Volume of a Prism
author: Becky Allen
summary: Becky Allen uses a single classroom case — teaching the volume of a prism — to make a broader argument about the limits of instructional theory. Two designers working from the same Direct Instruction principles produced two lesson sequences of visibly different quality, which Allen takes as proof that a theory can specify constraints without specifying the winning design. She credits Kris Boulton's superior sequencing not to a more faithful application of theory but to years of classroom experience noticing how students actually respond, which theory alone cannot supply. Allen argues that Direct Instruction's own history bears this out: its founding programs were not derived logically from first principles but built through repeated field-testing and revision against real student errors. The piece lands on a modest but pointed conclusion for curriculum design: principled frameworks are necessary for narrowing the space of reasonable lessons, but the actual choice within that space is an act of expert judgment, not a further deduction from theory.
points: Allen's central claim — 'Between its principles and his finished design lies a wide space of acceptable lessons' — reframes curriculum design as a judgment problem that theory constrains but does not solve, a useful corrective for anyone treating a pedagogical framework as a recipe.

By tracing Kris Boulton's superior sequencing to accumulated classroom experience rather than more rigorous theory-application, Allen locates real instructional expertise in tacit, practice-built knowledge that resists being fully written down.

Her reminder that even canonical Direct Instruction programs were built through 'relentless field tested and revised' iteration — not pure theoretical derivation — challenges curriculum writers to treat field-testing as indispensable, not as a lesser substitute for getting the theory right.
